estimated_study_time.text: Plan to spend about 2 hours on this chapter, with time for reading the item descriptions, practising fill-in-the-blanks strategies, building vocabulary tables, and reviewing answers.

chapter_summary.text: This lesson focuses on Reading: Fill in the blanks and Reading & writing: Fill in the blanks. It develops reading skills such as identifying main ideas, using context, understanding academic vocabulary, inferring unfamiliar words, and following logical sequence, alongside writing skills such as using appropriate words, correct grammar, and correct spelling. Learners analyze the rubric, format, scoring, and strategies for these item types, complete timed practice items, review feedback, and practise vocabulary skills.

core_lessons.title: Use Grammar And Context To Choose Missing Words

explanation.text: To choose the correct words in fill-in-the-blanks texts, use the grammatical context of a word, combine words into logical phrases, and eliminate words that do not make grammatical or lexical sense.

evidence_spans.quote:
Using the grammatical context of a word (e.g. ‘tests’ is a verb that follows and agrees with the 
subject ‘item’).

Combining words so that they make logical phrases (e.g. the phrase ‘  to five blanks’ needs 
another number at its beginning).
Some words, such as ‘question’, make neither grammatical nor lexical sense

core_lessons.title: Use Word Classes To Narrow The Options

explanation.text: The grammatical context of a word or phrase can show which word classes are needed. For example, a phrase may require a modifying adjective, while the infinitive “to” may require a verb in its base form.

core_lessons.title: Use Dictionaries And Thesauruses For Vocabulary Work

explanation.text: Use a dictionary to check grammatical forms, word endings, and collocations. Use a thesaurus to check synonyms and antonyms.

worked_examples.title: Eliminating Words That Do Not Fit

example.text: Blank: “The research team will _____ the data after collection.” Options: analyze, make, concern, party. A learner eliminates “party” and “concern” because they do not fit the grammatical or lexical context, and chooses “analyze” because it combines logically with “data.”

explanation.text: This example applies two lesson strategies: eliminating words that do not make grammatical or lexical sense, and using logical collocation. The lesson also states that documentation, data, and results can be analyzed and read.

misconception.text: The verb “make” collocates with the research nouns in the research collocation table.

correction.text: The research nouns do not all combine with every verb. Documentation, data, and results can be analyzed and read, but not conducted or done. Research and studies refer to the whole research process rather than individual aspects.

question.text: In a Reading: Fill in the blanks task, what three checks should you make before choosing a word for a blank?

answer.text: Check the grammatical context, check whether the word combines with nearby words to make a logical phrase, and eliminate words that do not make grammatical or lexical sense.

question.text: Create a small word bank for the topic “research.” Include at least one noun form, one verb form, one synonym or related word, and one collocation.

answer.text: A useful answer should organize vocabulary into categories such as noun forms, verb forms, synonyms, antonyms, and collocations. For example, a learner might include “research” as a noun, “to research” as a verb, and a collocation such as “conduct research.”

question.text: Choose the better answer: “The student looked _____ the word in a dictionary.” Options: on, out, up. Explain your choice.

answer.text: The better answer is “up”: “look up” can mean to look up a word in a dictionary.

question.text: After completing a fill-in-the-blanks practice item, write two sentences explaining how you used collocation or phrasal verb knowledge to choose or eliminate an answer.

answer.text: A strong answer names the nearby words, explains why one option forms a logical or idiomatic phrase, and explains why another option was eliminated.

review_checklist.text: I can explain the difference between the two fill-in-the-blanks item types covered in this lesson.
I can use grammatical context to decide what kind of word is needed in a blank.
I can identify logical, common, or idiomatic phrases by checking collocations.
I can eliminate options that do not make grammatical or lexical sense.
I can build a word bank with grammatical forms, synonyms, antonyms, and collocations.
I can use a phrasal verb table to check whether a verb and preposition form an idiomatic phrasal verb.
